summary: SE-led deep dive into KV cache shard pressure, prefix reuse, and prefetching strategy. Customer runs on VPC with sensitive genomic prompts; goal is to reduce tail latency and avoid KV spill to disk during bursty batch workloads. Discussed quantization effects on cache hit distribution and a proposed repro + pilot path.
topics: hot shard pressure under bursty batch traffic
prefix reuse across sessions and long-context stitch
KV paging/spill behavior and disk I/O impacts
VPC networking constraints and on-prem pilot considerations
quantized model interaction with KV cache (8-bit behavior)
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Park (AtlasGenomics), Rajiv Menon (Atlas SRE), Sofia Alvarez (Product)

Auto-summary (auto): Customer seeing intermittent 500ms+ tail latency during burst inference; suspects hot-prefix hotspots causing KV spill and increased disk IO; exploring prefetch heuristics + shard rebalancing and quantized model side-effects.

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros then Jonah will lead the technical reproduction. Elena, do you want to kick off with the customer problem in one minute?

[00:22] Dr. Elena Park: Yeah sure. So basically we ingest clinical notes, long multi-turn transcripts, and we get these spikes where latency jumps and throughput drops, we've traced some to the session store basically - the kv cache - values are getting paged out and then the GPU sits waiting while disk reads happen. It's intermittent, kind of correlated with some prefixes that are reused a lot, and also during our nightly batch enrichment where we blast a few hundred concurrent streams.

[00:48] Rajiv (SRE): plus we run inside a VPC with tight egress, so any additional network hops to a managed service are tricky. We're considering Redwood Dedicated or Private, but we need to understand the KV behavior first.

[01:05] Jonah (SE): Okay that's helpful. Quick question — when you say "paged out" do you mean to local NVMe spill or across the network to a backing store?

[01:14] Dr. Elena Park: Local NVMe, mostly. On our test nodes we see disk spikes and iowait. On some instances we observed prefix reuse leading to a burst of cache misses on the same shard.

[01:30] Jonah (SE): Got it. The thing we'll want to check is hot-shard concentration. If too many prefixes map to the same slab, you get eviction churn, and prefetch heuristics may not be aggressive enough. Also quantized models can change the sequence length distribution so the KV lookups pattern may change — 8-bit models tend to emit slightly different tokenization which can increase prefix variance.

[01:52] Dr. Elena Park: Wait — quantization changes tokenization? We didn't expect that.

[01:57] Jonah (SE): Sorry, I should be clearer. Quantization doesn't change the tokenizer but it can subtly alter generation distributions; for instance, different logits can lead to different continuation choices which over many sessions changes which prefixes become hot. It's a statistical effect, not a tokenizer-level change.

[02:20] Sofia (Product): For our prioritization: tail latency under 300ms is "good", 300-700ms is tolerable, above 700ms is a hard blocker for our users. We're seeing intermittent >1s tails.

[02:36] Maya (AE): Thanks. Jonah, do you want to walk through the repro plan and the telemetry we need?

[02:45] Jonah (SE): Sure. Step one: collect KV metrics around per-shard hit/miss rates, eviction rate, spill-to-disk counts, and slow disk IO latencies for the window where you see the spikes. We also want per-prefix appearance counts so we can detect prefix reuse concentration. If possible, capture a 60-90s flamegraph of the runtime's memalloc and KV ops.

[03:12] Rajiv (SRE): We can pull those. We have a custom exporter for node-level metrics, but we might not have application-level per-prefix counts instrumented in production. We can enable a debug mode on a staging pool.

[03:28] Jonah (SE): Staging pool is perfect. Also enable KV debug logging for a short window — we realize that adds overhead, but for triage it's fine. We'll provide the commands to toggle.

[03:42] Dr. Elena Park: One more nuance — we shard by user ID mod N, but some enterprise customers batch many users together so certain shards get heavy reuse. Could shard hashing or affinity be part of the problem?

[03:58] Jonah (SE): Absolutely. Hash skew is a classic cause. Two mitigation paths: re-hash to more shards to reduce collision probability, or add a lightweight routing layer that tries to spread concurrent sessions across multiple shard groups. Both have tradeoffs — re-hash requires migration or double-writing; routing adds complexity.

[04:20] Maya (AE): Cost/ops tradeoff question: which is faster to test?

[04:25] Jonah (SE): Re-hashing a staging pool is quickest for an experiment: increase shard count from, say, 256 to 1024 and run the batch to see if per-shard load drops. But that will increase meta-data memory. Routing is more surgical but needs changes to request routing layer.

[04:44] Sofia (Product): If we increase shard count, does that affect latency for cold prefixes?

[04:49] Jonah (SE): Slightly. More shards means more granular caching so cold prefixes may be distributed, but it shouldn't materially increase tail latency. The big win is reducing eviction churn on hot shards so you avoid repeated disk reads.

[05:05] Dr. Elena Park: We also saw a case where a prefix had a large serialized object that made the slab fill faster — might be due to embedding vectors being included in the session payload. Any suggestions?

[05:20] Jonah (SE): If the session payload mixes embeddings or large blobs with KV entries, we recommend separating heavy value payloads into a separate storage tier and keep the KV cache for lightweight context. Ridge approach: compress or downsample stored vectors and switch to pointer references in the cache.

[05:38] Rajiv (SRE): Regarding disk iowait, our NVMe is on a shared host. If the KV spills frequently during bursts, we see queue depth spike and other tenants are affected. That is why we're leaning toward Private.

[05:50] Maya (AE): Understood. Private would let you size NVMe and isolate IO, but it comes with ops overhead. Jonah, any quant-specific observations?

[05:58] Jonah (SE): Yes — two notes: 1) quantized 8-bit execution paths can alter per-token compute time slightly which changes the timing between KV lookups and may increase simultaneous outstanding KV accesses; 2) smaller model footprints allow denser batching which can shift the distribution of cache accesses per second. In practice that means sometimes a q8 model increases short-term concurrency and stresses the cache differently.

[06:27] Dr. Elena Park: So switching to q8 could either help or make things worse depending on batching?

[06:33] Jonah (SE): Exactly. That's why we want an A/B run: run a q16 baseline and a q8 variant under the same workload and compare hit rates and disk IO.

[06:45] [07:00] Elena (customer): We can do that in staging, we have both model artifacts.

[07:05] Jonah (SE): Great. Next, prefetch heuristics: current Redwood prefetch is prefix-based with two modes — conservative and aggressive. For your workload, conservative misses hot-prefix turnover; aggressive increases memory pressure. There's an intermediate approach: adaptive-prefetch that monitors per-prefix reuse velocity and only prefetch prefixes that show rising reuse within a short window.

[07:34] Rajiv (SRE): What's a good threshold for "rising reuse"?

[07:38] Jonah (SE): Our rule-of-thumb is more than X hits across Y seconds where X and Y are tunable. For your batch bursts, something like 10 hits in 30 seconds indicates rising hotness. We'll propose numbers after seeing telemetry.

[07:54] Sofia (Product): Can we combine adaptive-prefetch with TTL bumping so hot prefixes keep a slightly longer residency?

[08:01] Jonah (SE): Yes, bumping TTL for detected hot prefixes is low-risk and often very effective. The key is to avoid bumping everything; we only bump when reuse velocity surpasses threshold and when slab pressure is below an upper bound.

[08:18] [08:30] Dr. Elena Park: We worry about TTL bumping causing memory growth over time. What's the mechanism to retract bumps?

[08:36] Jonah (SE): Bumps are time-limited; we set a max bump window and also track decreasing reuse velocity. Once reuse drops, TTL reverts. There's also an eviction priority that favors recently bumped hot prefixes but still allows eviction if overall memory pressure is high.

[08:54] Rajiv (SRE): Could prefetch and TTL bump together cause a feedback loop — prefetch causes hits which cause bumps which keep the prefix resident forever?

[09:05] Jonah (SE): It can in pathological configs. That's why we cap aggregate memory reserved for bumped prefixes and add a decay factor. We'll share the config knobs.

[09:18] Maya (AE): Let's talk about instrumentation. What exact traces/logs do you need from our runtime?

[09:24] Jonah (SE): Per-shard metrics, per-prefix counters (at least sampled), eviction events with timestamps and cause, spill-to-disk counters with IO latency percentiles, and request-level correlation IDs so we can join upstream traces. If possible, CPU and GPU queue depth metrics to correlate timing.

[09:45] [10:00] Dr. Elena Park: We'll enable sampling for prefix counters in staging and collect a 30 minute window around a simulated burst.

[10:08] Jonah (SE): Perfect. For reproduction, we want to run a synthetic workload that mimics your nightly enrichment: 300 concurrent streams, 60s average prompt length with bursts that include repeating prefixes. We'll provide a harness you can run in your cluster.

[10:25] Sofia (Product): About routing/re-hash: migration cost is a concern. Is there an incremental migration option?

[10:32] Jonah (SE): We support dual-write for a transition window — writes go to both hash spaces and reads prefer the new shard mapping when present. That reduces risk but increases write load temporarily. It's what we recommend for live migration.

[10:46] Rajiv (SRE): For Private deployment, do you support static shard placement to specific NVMe nodes so we can isolate high-IO shards?

[10:55] Jonah (SE): Yes, Private allows you to pin shard ranges to specific devices and you can choose NVMe sizing per node. That's a larger ops change but gives deterministic IO isolation.

[11:10] Dr. Elena Park: Any recommendations on batch sizing and batching window to avoid overloading KV?

[11:16] Jonah (SE): Try smaller batching windows during bursts — e.g., reduce max batch tokens from 2048 to 1024 — that reduces concurrent outstanding KV lookups. Also implement back-pressure so if KV latency rises, you pause aggressive batching.

[11:32] [11:45] Maya (AE): This is great. I'm going to summarize the proposed short-term experiments. Jonah?

[11:48] Jonah (SE): Short-term experiments: 1) Run telemetry capture in staging during a simulated burst (per-shard, per-prefix sampled counters). 2) Repro: increase shard count in staging to observe change in per-shard load. 3) A/B q16 vs q8 under identical workload to see concurrency and cache impact. 4) Try adaptive-prefetch + TTL bump in a small canary pool. We'll provide the config and test harness.

[12:15] Dr. Elena Park: Sounds reasonable. For the A/B tests, we'd like to keep everything else constant — same batch sizes, same routing.

[12:22] Jonah (SE): Absolutely. We'll give a checklist.

[12:27] Sofia (Product): From a compliance perspective: we need KMS integration and audit logs for Private. Maya, can you include compliance docs?

[12:34] Maya (AE): Yes — I'll attach SOC2, encryption at rest descriptions, and the KMS integration guide. Cliff note: Private supports customer KMS and audit logs for KV ops.

[12:48] Rajiv (SRE): One more: what's the recommended spill threshold to NVMe before we trigger early prefetch or aggressiveness?

[12:55] Jonah (SE): We treat spill rate > 0.1% of ops/sec sustained as a signal to shift to aggressive mitigation: TTL bumping + temporary prefetch. But exact numbers need tuning per workload.

[13:10] [13:30] Dr. Elena Park: Can you share an example prefetch config we can test?

[13:35] Jonah (SE): We'll share a sample YAML: parameters for velocity threshold, bump window, max bumped memory percent, and sample rate for prefix instrumentation. We'll also include a script to replay sampled prefixes to validate correctness.

[13:52] Maya (AE): Competitor question — you mentioned GigaServe earlier, Rajiv said they considered them. Any differentiator we should call out?

[13:59] Jonah (SE): Quick point: some vendors rely on coarse LRU slab eviction which can exacerbate hot-shard churn. Redwood supports adaptive-prefetch and TTL bumping as first-class features plus Private pinning. We'll send a short comparison doc.

[14:20] Sofia (Product): Timeline — if the repro shows a clear improvement, we'd like to run a 2-week pilot in Private. Is that feasible?

[14:27] Maya (AE): Yes — pilot timelines depend on procurement but technically yes; we'll include pilot duration and costs in the follow-up.

[14:35] Jonah (SE): Implementation notes: for the adaptive-prefetch canary we'll start with 10% of sessions routed to the canary pool to validate no negative impact.

[14:47] [15:00] Dr. Elena Park: A couple of practicalities — we'll need the enable/disable flags for debug logging and the exact metrics names so our exporter can scrape.

[15:06] Jonah (SE): We'll send the exact metric names and a toggle script. Also will include instructions to turn on sampled prefix counters and how to upload logs securely (S3 presigned or direct sftp into a redwood ingestion bucket).

[15:25] Rajiv (SRE): Security note — we require SAML SSO and scoped API keys for ingestion endpoints. Does Redwood support scoped keys for telemetry?

[15:35] Maya (AE): Yes, scoped short-lived keys and SSO can be supported. We'll include the onboarding doc.

[15:45] Jonah (SE): A quick caution: when collecting prefix samples, scrub PII. If sample payloads include genomic identifiers, ensure redaction before sending.

[15:56] Dr. Elena Park: We'll redact identifiers and share the prompt patterns only.

[16:03] [16:30] Maya (AE): Great. Any outstanding concerns?

[16:05] Sofia (Product): Just on cost — if we increase shard count or run Private with bigger NVMe, what's rough ballpark? Maya you'll follow up?

[16:11] Maya (AE): I'll include a delta estimate in the follow-up.

[16:18] Jonah (SE): Ok final technical recap: collect telemetry, run shard scaling experiment, run q8 vs q16 A/B, enable adaptive-prefetch in a canary, and review results. If eviction still high, consider shard pinning or migrating to Private with isolated NVMe.

[16:38] [16:50] Dr. Elena Park: Thanks Jonah, Maya. We'll schedule a follow-up after we run the staging harness — aim for next week.

[16:56] Maya (AE): Perfect. I'll send notes and the configs.

[17:00] End of call.
